lessons.title: Getting Started with Docker
lessons.description: Understand what Docker is, why it exists, and run your first container.

blocks.content: Getting Started with Docker

Docker solves the 'it works on my machine' problem. It packages your application and its dependencies into a single, portable container that runs identically on any machine — your laptop, a colleague's computer, or a production server. Every modern tech company uses Docker for deployment.

Docker is a platform for developing, shipping, and running applications in containers. A container is a lightweight, standalone, executable package that includes everything needed to run an application: code, runtime, system tools, libraries, and settings.

items: Basic command-line/terminal familiarity
A computer running Windows, macOS, or Linux
No prior Docker or container experience needed
What is a container vs a virtual machine?
Installing Docker Desktop
The docker command-line interface
Running your first container: hello-world
Understanding images vs containers

blocks.code:
# Check Docker is installed
docker --version
# Run your first container
docker run hello-world

# List running containers
docker ps
# List all containers (including stopped)
docker ps -a
# List downloaded images
docker images
blocks.caption: Basic Docker commands

items: Image: a read-only template with instructions for creating a container (like a class in OOP)
Container: a runnable instance of an image (like an object in OOP)
Docker Engine: the runtime that builds and runs containers
Docker Hub: the public registry where images are stored (like GitHub for containers)
Forgetting to stop and remove old containers — they accumulate and waste disk space
Running containers as root by default — for production, create a non-root user
Not understanding that containers are ephemeral — data inside a container is lost when it stops; use volumes for persistence
What's the difference between a Docker image and a container?
How does Docker differ from a virtual machine?
What is Docker Hub and why is it useful?

blocks.content: Run the nginx web server in a container and access it in your browser: docker run -d -p 8080:80 nginx, then open http://localhost:8080

items: Run the ubuntu container interactively: docker run -it ubuntu bash
List all containers on your system and clean up stopped ones with docker container prune

quiz.question: What is the key difference between a Docker image and a container?
options: An image is a running process; a container is a file
An image is a read-only template; a container is a running instance of it
A container is a template; an image is a running instance
quiz.explanation: An image is the blueprint (read-only template), and a container is a running instance created from that image — like a class vs an object in OOP.

quiz.question: Which command runs a container from the hello-world image?
quiz.explanation: docker run creates AND starts a container from an image. docker create only creates it; docker start starts an existing container.

quiz.question: What happens to data inside a container when the container stops?
options: It's automatically saved to Docker Hub
It's lost unless you use a volume
It's saved to the host's /tmp directory
quiz.explanation: Containers are ephemeral — data written inside the container filesystem is lost when the container is removed. Use Docker volumes or bind mounts for data that needs to persist.

quiz.question: Which command lists all running containers?
quiz.explanation: docker ps lists running containers. Use docker ps -a to include stopped containers.

quiz.question: What is Docker Hub?
options: A public registry for Docker images
quiz.explanation: Docker Hub is the default public registry where Docker images are stored and shared — like GitHub but for container images.

lessons.title: Dockerfile Basics — Building Custom Images
lessons.description: Write a Dockerfile to package your application into a custom Docker image.

blocks.content: Dockerfile Basics — Building Custom Images

A Dockerfile is how you package your own application into a reproducible, portable Docker image. It's the bridge between 'my code on my laptop' and 'my app running anywhere.' Every deployed containerized application starts with a Dockerfile.
A Dockerfile is a text file containing a series of instructions that Docker reads to build an image. Each instruction creates a new layer in the image, making builds cacheable and efficient.

items: Complete the 'Getting Started with Docker' lesson
Basic understanding of your application's dependencies
Dockerfile syntax: FROM, RUN, COPY, CMD
Building images with docker build
Tagging images
Best practices: .dockerignore, layer caching

blocks.code:
# Dockerfile for a simple Node.js app
FROM node:20-alpine

WORKDIR /app

# Copy package files and install dependencies first (for caching)
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --production

# Copy the rest of the application
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app runs on
EXPOSE 3000

# Command to run the application
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
blocks.caption: A typical Node.js Dockerfile

items: FROM: the base image to build on (e.g., node:20, python:3.12, ubuntu:22.04)
RUN: executes a command during the build (e.g., npm install)
COPY: copies files from your machine into the image
CMD: the default command to run when the container starts
Layer caching: each instruction creates a layer; Docker caches layers so rebuilds are fast
Copying all files before npm install — this invalidates the cache every time code changes, making rebuilds slow
Using :latest tag — it's unpredictable; always pin a specific version
Running as root — create a non-root user in the Dockerfile for security
What does the FROM instruction do in a Dockerfile?
Why would you COPY package.json and RUN npm install before copying the rest of the code?
What's the difference between CMD and ENTRYPOINT?

blocks.content: Write a Dockerfile for a simple Python Flask app, build it with docker build -t my-flask-app ., and run it with docker run -p 5000:5000 my-flask-app

items: Create a .dockerignore file to exclude node_modules, .git, and other unnecessary files from the build context
Add a HEALTHCHECK instruction to your Dockerfile

quiz.question: What does the FROM instruction in a Dockerfile do?
options: Sets the base image to build on
quiz.explanation: FROM specifies the base image — every Dockerfile starts with FROM (e.g., FROM node:20-alpine).

quiz.question: Why should you COPY package.json and RUN npm install BEFORE copying the rest of your code?
options: For layer caching — dependencies only reinstall when package.json changes
quiz.explanation: Docker caches layers. By installing dependencies before copying code, the expensive npm install layer is cached and only re-runs when package.json changes — not on every code change.

quiz.question: Which instruction sets the default command to run when the container starts?
quiz.explanation: CMD sets the default command. It can be overridden at runtime with docker run <image> <command>.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of a .dockerignore file?
options: To exclude files from the build context (like .gitignore for Docker)
quiz.explanation: .dockerignore excludes files/directories from the build context, making builds faster and images smaller (e.g., exclude node_modules, .git, .env).

quiz.question: Why should you avoid using the :latest tag in production?
options: It's unpredictable — the image it points to can change over time
quiz.explanation: The :latest tag is a moving target — it can point to different images over time. Always pin a specific version (e.g., node:20.11-alpine) for reproducible builds.

lessons.title: Docker Compose — Multi-Container Apps
lessons.description: Define and run multi-container applications with Docker Compose.

blocks.content: Docker Compose — Multi-Container Apps

Real applications rarely run in a single container — they need a database, a cache, maybe a queue. Docker Compose lets you define all of these in one file and start them with a single command. It's the standard way to run development environments.

Docker Compose is a tool for defining and running multi-container Docker applications. You write a docker-compose.yml file that describes your services, networks, and volumes, then run docker compose up to start everything.

items: Complete 'Getting Started with Docker' and 'Dockerfile Basics'
Basic understanding of YAML
docker-compose.yml syntax
Defining services, networks, and volumes
Environment variables and secrets
docker compose up / down / logs
Development vs production overrides

blocks.code:
# docker-compose.yml for a web app + database
services:
  web:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
    environment:
      - DATABASE_URL=postgres://user:pass@db:5432/myapp
    depends_on:
      - db

  db:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: user
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: pass
      POSTGRES_DB: myapp
    volumes:
      - db-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data

volumes:
  db-data:
blocks.caption: A typical docker-compose.yml

items: Service: a container defined in the compose file (e.g., web, db)
depends_on: controls startup order (db starts before web)
Volumes: persistent storage that survives container removal
Networks: services on the same network can reach each other by service name (e.g., db:5432)
depends_on doesn't wait for the database to be 'ready' — use a healthcheck or wait-for-it script
Not using named volumes — data is lost when you run docker compose down -v
Hardcoding secrets in the compose file — use .env files and docker secrets
How does Docker Compose differ from plain Docker?
What does depends_on do, and what does it NOT do?
How do services in a compose file communicate with each other?

blocks.content: Create a docker-compose.yml for a web app + PostgreSQL database. Start it with docker compose up, verify the web app can connect to the database, then stop it with docker compose down.

items: Add a Redis cache service to your compose file
Use a docker-compose.override.yml file for development-specific settings

quiz.question: What is Docker Compose used for?
quiz.explanation: Docker Compose defines and runs multi-container applications — e.g., a web server + database + cache — all from a single YAML file.

quiz.question: How do services in a compose file communicate with each other?
quiz.explanation: Services on the same Docker network can reach each other by service name. For example, the web service can connect to the database at db:5432 — Docker's built-in DNS resolves the service name.

quiz.question: What does depends_on do?
options: Waits for a service to be healthy
quiz.explanation: depends_on controls startup ORDER — the database container starts before the web container. But it does NOT wait for the database to be 'ready to accept connections.' Use a healthcheck or a wait-for-it script for that.

quiz.question: Which command starts all services defined in docker-compose.yml?
quiz.explanation: docker compose up builds, (re)creates, starts, and attaches to all services. Use -d for detached mode (running in background).

quiz.question: What is a Docker volume used for in a compose file?
options: For persistent data that survives container removal
quiz.explanation: Volumes provide persistent storage. Without a volume, data inside the database container is lost when the container is removed. Named volumes (e.g., db-data:) persist across docker compose down/up cycles.

lessons.title: Docker Volumes & Data Persistence
lessons.description: Persist data across container restarts with Docker volumes and bind mounts.

blocks.content: Docker Volumes & Data Persistence

Containers are ephemeral — when a container is removed, all data inside it is lost. For databases, user uploads, logs, or any data that must survive, you need volumes. Understanding persistence is essential for running any stateful application in Docker.
Docker provides two main ways to persist data: named volumes (managed by Docker) and bind mounts (mapped to a host directory). Each has trade-offs for development vs production.

items: Complete 'Getting Started with Docker'
Basic understanding of filesystems
Named volumes vs bind mounts
Creating and managing volumes
Sharing volumes between containers
Backup and restore strategies

blocks.code:
# Create a named volume
docker volume create my-data

# Use a volume in a container
docker run -d \
  --name my-db \
  -v my-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data \
  postgres:16

# List volumes
docker volume ls

# Inspect a volume
docker volume inspect my-data

# Remove a volume (only if no container is using it)
docker volume rm my-data

# Bind mount (maps a host directory into the container)
docker run -v /host/path:/container/path my-image
blocks.caption: Docker volume commands

items: Named volume: managed by Docker, stored in a Docker-managed location on the host
Bind mount: maps a specific host directory into the container — great for development (live code reload)
Volume driver: plugins that let volumes be stored on remote hosts or cloud storage (e.g., NFS, AWS EBS)
Using bind mounts in production — they create a coupling between the host filesystem and the container; use named volumes instead
Forgetting to back up volumes — use docker run --rm -v my-data:/data -v $(pwd):/backup ubuntu tar cvf /backup/my-data.tar /data to back up
Running docker volume rm on a volume that's in use — Docker will warn you; always stop containers first
What's the difference between a named volume and a bind mount?
How would you back up a Docker volume?
When would you use a bind mount vs a named volume?

blocks.content: Run a PostgreSQL container with a named volume. Insert some data, stop and remove the container, start a new container with the same volume, and verify the data is still there.

items: Back up a volume to a tar file and restore it to a new volume
Share a volume between two containers simultaneously

quiz.question: What is the key difference between a named volume and a bind mount?
options: Named volumes are managed by Docker; bind mounts map a specific host directory
quiz.explanation: Named volumes are created and managed by Docker (stored in Docker's area on the host). Bind mounts map a specific host directory into the container — you specify the exact path on the host.

quiz.question: Why are containers described as 'ephemeral'?
options: Data inside a container is lost when the container is removed
quiz.explanation: Ephemeral means 'lasting for a very short time.' When a container is removed, its writable layer (where all runtime data is stored) is deleted. Volumes solve this by storing data outside the container's filesystem.

quiz.question: Which flag mounts a volume into a container?
quiz.explanation: The -v (or --volume) flag mounts a volume. Syntax: -v volume-name:/container/path or -v /host/path:/container/path for bind mounts.

quiz.question: When would you use a bind mount instead of a named volume?
options: In development for live code reloading
quiz.explanation: Bind mounts are great for development — you map your source code directory into the container, and changes on the host are immediately reflected inside the container (live reload). For production, use named volumes.

quiz.question: How do you back up a Docker volume?
options: Run a temporary container that mounts the volume and creates a tar archive
quiz.explanation: To back up a volume, run a temporary container that mounts both the volume and a host directory, then creates a tar archive: docker run --rm -v my-data:/data -v $(pwd):/backup ubuntu tar cvf /backup/backup.tar /data

lessons.title: Docker Best Practices & Optimization
lessons.description: Optimize Docker images for size, security, and build speed with multi-stage builds and best practices.

blocks.content: Docker Best Practices & Optimization

A poorly written Dockerfile produces large images, slow builds, and security vulnerabilities. Production Docker images should be small (faster to pull), secure (fewer attack surfaces), and cacheable (fast rebuilds). These best practices are what separate casual Docker users from professionals.
Multi-stage builds, alpine base images, layer optimization, and non-root users are the key techniques for production-grade Docker images.

items: Complete 'Dockerfile Basics' and 'Docker Compose'
Basic understanding of Linux permissions
Multi-stage builds
Choosing the right base image (alpine vs slim vs full)
Layer optimization and caching
Security: non-root users, minimal images, scanning
docker scan and Docker Scout

blocks.code:
# Multi-stage build for a Node.js app

# Stage 1: Build
FROM node:20-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

# Stage 2: Production
FROM node:20-alpine AS production
WORKDIR /app

# Create a non-root user
RUN addgroup -g 1001 -S nodejs && \
    adduser -S nextjs -u 1001

# Copy only production dependencies
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --production && npm cache clean --force

# Copy the built app from the builder stage
COPY --from=builder /app/dist ./dist

# Switch to non-root user
USER nodejs

EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]
blocks.caption: Multi-stage Dockerfile with non-root user

items: Multi-stage build: use multiple FROM instructions; only the final stage ends up in the image (smaller image, no build tools in production)
Alpine: a tiny Linux distribution (~5MB) — use node:20-alpine instead of node:20 for much smaller images
Non-root user: containers run as root by default; create and switch to a non-root user for security
Layer squashing: each RUN/COPY creates a layer; combine RUN commands to reduce layers
Using full OS images (ubuntu:22.04 is ~77MB) when alpine would do (~5MB) — 15x larger than needed
Leaving build tools (gcc, make, devDependencies) in the production image — increases size and attack surface
Not scanning images for vulnerabilities — use docker scout or trivy to find CVEs in your base image
What is a multi-stage build and why would you use it?
How can you reduce the size of a Docker image?
Why should you run containers as a non-root user?

blocks.content: Take an existing single-stage Dockerfile and convert it to a multi-stage build. Compare the image sizes with docker images before and after.

items: Scan your image with docker scout to find vulnerabilities
Use a .dockerignore to exclude unnecessary files and measure the build time improvement

quiz.question: What is the main benefit of a multi-stage build?
options: Smaller final image — only the final stage's content is included
quiz.explanation: Multi-stage builds let you use a 'builder' stage with all build tools, then copy only the built artifacts into a clean final stage. The build tools and intermediate files don't end up in the production image — it's much smaller.

quiz.question: Why use node:20-alpine instead of node:20?
quiz.explanation: Alpine Linux is ~5MB vs ~100MB for a full Debian-based image. Using alpine base images dramatically reduces image size and pull time.

quiz.question: Why should containers run as a non-root user?
options: Security — if an attacker breaks in, they have limited permissions
quiz.explanation: By default, containers run as root. If an attacker exploits a vulnerability in your app, they get root access inside the container. Creating and switching to a non-root user limits the damage.

quiz.question: Which tool scans Docker images for known vulnerabilities?
quiz.explanation: docker scout (formerly docker scan) and third-party tools like trivy scan images against CVE databases and report known vulnerabilities in the base image and installed packages.

quiz.question: How do you combine multiple RUN commands to reduce layers?
options: Chain with && in a single RUN instruction
quiz.explanation: Each RUN creates a layer. Combine them: RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* — this creates one layer instead of three.

lessons.title: Docker Volumes & Persistent Data
lessons.description: Learn how to persist data across container restarts using Docker volumes and bind mounts.

blocks.content: Docker Volumes & Persistent Data
Without volumes, all data is lost when a container is removed. Volumes are essential for databases, file uploads, and any stateful application.

items: Complete Docker lessons 01-15 first.
Volume types (named, anonymous, bind mounts)
Creating and managing volumes
Sharing data between containers
Backup and restore strategies
Volumes are managed by Docker and survive container removal
Bind mounts link host directories to containers
tmpfs mounts store data in host memory only

blocks.code:
# Create a named volume
docker volume create mydata

# Use it in a container
docker run -v mydata:/app/data myimage

# Inspect a volume
docker volume inspect mydata

# List volumes
docker volume ls

# Remove unused volumes
docker volume prune
blocks.caption: Docker volume commands

blocks.content: Docker volumes are the preferred mechanism for persisting data generated by and used by Docker containers. While bind mounts are dependent on the directory structure of the host machine, volumes are completely managed by Docker.

items: Forgetting to mount volumes loses all data on container removal
Using bind mounts in production can cause permission issues
Not backing up volumes before operations
Database persistence in containerized apps
Sharing config files between containers
CI/CD artifact caching
What is the difference between a volume and a bind mount?
How do you back up a Docker volume?
When would you use tmpfs mounts?

blocks.content: Create a container that writes logs to a named volume, then start a second container that reads those logs from the same volume.

items: Create a named volume and inspect it
Run a container with a bind mount
Share a volume between two containers

quiz.question: What happens to data stored in a container's filesystem when the container is removed?
options: It moves to the host filesystem
quiz.explanation: Container filesystems are ephemeral — data is lost when the container is removed unless stored in a volume.

quiz.question: Which Docker volume type is managed by Docker and survives container removal?
quiz.explanation: Named volumes are created and managed by Docker, independent of the host directory structure.

quiz.question: What command creates a named volume?
quiz.explanation: The correct syntax is 'docker volume create <name>'.

quiz.question: How do you mount a volume in a container?
quiz.explanation: The -v flag mounts a volume: -v <volume_name>:<container_path>.

quiz.question: What is a bind mount?
options: A link between a host directory and container path
quiz.explanation: Bind mounts directly map a host machine directory to a container path.

quiz.question: Which volume type stores data in host memory only?
quiz.explanation: tmpfs mounts store data in the host's memory (RAM), never writing to disk.

quiz.question: How do you list all Docker volumes?
quiz.explanation: The command 'docker volume ls' lists all volumes on the host.

quiz.question: What does 'docker volume prune' do?
quiz.explanation: docker volume prune removes volumes not currently used by any container.

quiz.question: Can multiple containers share the same volume?
options: No, only one container per volume
Yes, by mounting the same volume name
Only if they're on the same network
quiz.explanation: Multiple containers can mount the same named volume simultaneously.

quiz.question: What is the main advantage of named volumes over bind mounts?
options: They are managed by Docker and portable across hosts
quiz.explanation: Named volumes are managed by Docker, independent of host directory structure, making them portable.

lessons.title: Docker Networking Deep Dive
lessons.description: Master Docker networking: bridge, host, overlay, and custom networks for multi-container communication.

blocks.content: Docker Networking Deep Dive
Networking is how containers communicate with each other and the outside world. Understanding Docker networking is essential for multi-container applications.

items: Complete Docker lesson 16 first.
Network drivers (bridge, host, overlay, macvlan)
Creating custom networks
Container DNS and service discovery
Port mapping and exposure
Bridge is the default network driver
Custom networks provide automatic DNS resolution
Overlay networks span multiple Docker hosts

blocks.code:
# Create a custom network
docker network create mynet

# Run containers on the same network
docker run --network mynet --name api myimage
docker run --network mynet --name db myimage

# Containers can reach each other by name
# Inside 'api' container: ping db

# List networks
docker network ls

# Inspect a network
docker network inspect mynet

# Connect a running container to a network
docker network connect mynet existing_container
blocks.caption: Docker networking commands

blocks.content: Docker's networking subsystem is pluggable, using drivers. The default bridge network doesn't provide DNS resolution between containers. Custom bridge networks do — containers on the same custom network can reach each other by name.

items: Containers on different networks cannot communicate by default
Published ports (-p) expose ports to the host, not to other containers
Using host networking removes network isolation
Microservices communication
Service mesh setups
Isolating environments (dev/test/prod)
How does DNS resolution work in custom Docker networks?
What is the difference between bridge and overlay networks?
When would you use host networking?

blocks.content: Create a custom network, run two containers on it, and verify they can communicate using container names as hostnames.

items: Create a custom bridge network
Run two containers and ping by name
Inspect network details

quiz.question: What is the default Docker network driver?
quiz.explanation: The bridge network driver is the default for containers unless specified otherwise.

quiz.question: How do containers on a custom network discover each other?
options: Through automatic DNS resolution by container name
quiz.explanation: Custom bridge networks provide automatic DNS resolution — containers can reach each other by name.

quiz.question: What command creates a custom Docker network?
quiz.explanation: The command 'docker network create <name>' creates a custom network.

quiz.question: What does the -p flag do in 'docker run -p 8080:80'?
options: Maps container port 8080 to host port 80
Maps host port 8080 to container port 80
quiz.explanation: The -p flag maps a host port to a container port: -p <host_port>:<container_port>.

quiz.question: Can containers on different networks communicate by default?
options: Only if on the same host
quiz.explanation: Containers on different networks are isolated and cannot communicate unless connected to the same network.

quiz.question: What is an overlay network?
options: A network that spans multiple Docker hosts
A network on top of the host network
quiz.explanation: Overlay networks create a distributed network across multiple Docker hosts, enabling swarm communication.

quiz.question: How do you connect a running container to a network?
quiz.explanation: The 'docker network connect <network> <container>' command connects a running container to a network.

quiz.question: What is host networking?
options: A network that uses the host's network stack directly
A network for the Docker daemon
quiz.explanation: Host networking (--network host) makes the container use the host's network stack directly, removing isolation.

quiz.question: Why would you avoid host networking in production?
options: It removes network isolation and can cause port conflicts
quiz.explanation: Host networking removes container network isolation and can cause port conflicts with the host.

quiz.question: What does 'docker network inspect' show?
quiz.explanation: docker network inspect shows the network's configuration, IP range, and which containers are connected.

lessons.title: Docker Security Best Practices
lessons.description: Secure your Docker containers: image scanning, least privilege, secrets management, and runtime protection.

blocks.content: Docker Security Best Practices
Containers share the host kernel, so security vulnerabilities can affect the entire system. Following security best practices is critical for production deployments.

items: Complete Docker lesson 17 first.
Running as non-root user
Read-only filesystems
Image scanning and vulnerability detection
Docker secrets for sensitive data
Never run containers as root
Use multi-stage builds to reduce attack surface
Scan images with Trivy or Snyk

blocks.code:
# Run as non-root user
FROM node:20-alpine
RUN addgroup -S app && adduser -S app -G app
USER app

# Read-only filesystem
docker run --read-only myimage

# Use Docker secrets
echo "mysecret" | docker secret create db_password -

# Scan an image
trivy image myimage:latest
blocks.caption: Docker security practices

blocks.content: Container security involves multiple layers: the base image, the application code, the runtime configuration, and the host system. Each layer must be secured independently.

items: Running as root gives attackers full container access
Storing secrets in environment variables is visible via docker inspect
Not scanning images leaves known vulnerabilities
Compliance requirements (SOC2, PCI)
Multi-tenant container platforms
Supply chain security
What are Docker secrets and how do they differ from environment variables?
How do you reduce a Docker image's attack surface?
What is the principle of least privilege in containers?

blocks.content: Create a Dockerfile that runs as a non-root user, uses a read-only filesystem, and passes a security scan.

items: Create a non-root user in a Dockerfile
Run a container with --read-only
Scan an image with Trivy

quiz.question: Why should you avoid running containers as root?
options: It gives attackers full container access if compromised
quiz.explanation: Running as root means an attacker who compromises the container has root privileges, increasing the attack surface.

quiz.question: What does the USER instruction in a Dockerfile do?
options: Sets the user for running the container
quiz.explanation: The USER instruction sets the user (and optionally group) for instructions that follow it in the Dockerfile.

quiz.question: What does --read-only do when running a container?
quiz.explanation: The --read-only flag mounts the container's root filesystem as read-only, preventing writes to it.

quiz.question: How are Docker secrets different from environment variables?
options: Secrets are encrypted and not visible in docker inspect
quiz.explanation: Docker secrets are encrypted at rest and in transit, and are not visible in docker inspect or docker exec.

quiz.question: What tool can scan Docker images for vulnerabilities?
quiz.explanation: Both 'docker scan' (built-in) and 'trivy' (third-party) can scan images for known vulnerabilities.

quiz.question: What is a distroless image?
options: An image with no operating system
An image with only the runtime and application, no shell or package manager
An image without a base layer
quiz.explanation: Distroless images contain only your application and its runtime dependencies — no shell, package manager, or other tools.

quiz.question: How do multi-stage builds improve security?
options: By reducing the final image size and attack surface
quiz.explanation: Multi-stage builds copy only needed artifacts from build stages, excluding build tools and intermediate files from the final image.

quiz.question: What is the principle of least privilege in Docker?
options: Running containers with only the permissions they need
quiz.explanation: Least privilege means giving containers only the minimum capabilities and permissions needed to function.

quiz.question: What does 'docker scout' do?
options: Scans images for vulnerabilities and provides remediation advice
quiz.explanation: Docker Scout scans images for vulnerabilities, compares against base images, and suggests fixes.

quiz.question: Why should you avoid storing secrets in environment variables?
options: They're visible via docker inspect and in logs
quiz.explanation: Environment variables are visible in docker inspect, docker exec, and potentially in application logs.

lessons.title: Docker CI/CD Pipelines
lessons.description: Integrate Docker into CI/CD pipelines: build, test, scan, and push images automatically.

blocks.content: Docker CI/CD Pipelines
Automating Docker image builds and deployments in CI/CD ensures consistent, tested, and secure deployments.

items: Complete Docker lesson 18 first.
Building images in CI
Multi-architecture builds (buildx)
Image tagging strategies
Automated vulnerability scanning
Tag images with git commit SHA, not just 'latest'
Use buildx for multi-arch images
Cache layers in CI for faster builds

blocks.code:
# Build and tag
DOCKER_BUILDKIT=1 docker build \
  -t myregistry/app:${GIT_SHA} \
  -t myregistry/app:latest .

# Push
docker push myregistry/app:${GIT_SHA}
docker push myregistry/app:latest

# Multi-arch build
docker buildx build \
  --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 \
  -t myregistry/app:${GIT_SHA} \
  --push .
blocks.caption: CI/CD Docker commands

blocks.content: A good CI/CD pipeline for Docker should: build the image, run tests inside a container, scan for vulnerabilities, tag with semantic versioning or commit SHA, push to registry, and trigger deployment.

items: Using 'latest' tag exclusively makes rollbacks impossible
Not caching layers slows CI significantly
Not scanning before pushing risks deploying vulnerable images
GitHub Actions with Docker
GitLab CI container builds
Automated deployment pipelines
Why should you avoid using only the 'latest' tag in production?
What is Docker buildx and why is it useful?
How do you cache Docker layers in CI?

blocks.content: Set up a GitHub Actions workflow that builds, scans, and pushes a Docker image on every commit.

items: Build an image with a commit SHA tag
Set up layer caching in CI
Run a security scan in the pipeline

quiz.question: Why should you avoid using only the 'latest' tag in production?
options: It makes rollbacks impossible — you can't distinguish versions
quiz.explanation: Without unique tags (like commit SHA or version number), you can't identify or roll back to a specific version.

quiz.question: What is Docker buildx used for?
quiz.explanation: buildx enables building images for multiple CPU architectures simultaneously.

quiz.question: What should a CI/CD pipeline do after building a Docker image?
options: Run tests, scan for vulnerabilities, then push
quiz.explanation: A proper pipeline runs tests and security scans before pushing the image to a registry.

quiz.question: How do you cache Docker layers in GitHub Actions?
quiz.explanation: The docker/build-push-action supports cache-from and cache-to parameters for layer caching.

quiz.question: What is BuildKit?
options: A backend for building Docker images with better caching and parallelism
quiz.explanation: BuildKit is Docker's modern build backend that provides parallel builds, better caching, and multi-stage optimizations.

quiz.question: What is the best image tagging strategy?
quiz.explanation: Combining semantic version (v1.2.3) with commit SHA provides both human-readable and unique identifiers.

quiz.question: What does '--push' do in 'docker buildx build --push'?
options: Builds and pushes the image to a registry in one step
quiz.explanation: The --push flag builds the image and pushes it to the specified registry in a single command.

quiz.question: Why is layer caching important in CI?
options: It significantly speeds up builds by reusing unchanged layers
quiz.explanation: Layer caching avoids rebuilding unchanged layers, reducing build time from minutes to seconds.

quiz.question: What should you scan Docker images for in CI?
quiz.explanation: Scanning for known vulnerabilities (CVEs) ensures you don't deploy images with security issues.

quiz.question: What is a Docker registry?
options: A storage and distribution system for Docker images
quiz.explanation: A Docker registry stores and distributes Docker images (e.g., Docker Hub, GitHub Container Registry, ECR).

lessons.title: Multi-stage Builds & Image Optimization
lessons.description: Create smaller, more secure Docker images using multi-stage builds, distroless base images, and layer optimization.

blocks.content: Multi-stage Builds & Image Optimization
Smaller images are faster to build, push, pull, and deploy. They also have a smaller attack surface, improving security.

items: Complete Docker lesson 19 first.
Multi-stage build syntax
Choosing minimal base images (alpine, distroless)
Layer caching strategies
.dockerignore optimization
Multi-stage builds copy only needed artifacts from build stage
Distroless images have no shell, reducing attack surface
Order Dockerfile instructions from least to most frequently changing

blocks.code:
# Multi-stage build
FROM node:20 AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM node:20-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=builder /app/dist ./dist
COPY --from=builder /app/node_modules ./node_modules
CMD ["node", "dist/index.js"]
blocks.caption: Multi-stage Dockerfile

blocks.content: Multi-stage builds allow you to use multiple FROM statements in a single Dockerfile. Each FROM starts a new build stage. You can selectively copy artifacts from one stage to another, leaving behind everything you don't need in the final image.

items: Copying everything with COPY . . invalidates cache on every change
Large images slow deployment and increase attack surface
Not using .dockerignore includes unnecessary files
Reducing image size from 1GB to 50MB
Production-ready Node.js images
Go binary in scratch image
What is a distroless image and what are its benefits?
How does layer caching work in Docker?
What is the optimal Dockerfile instruction order?

blocks.content: Create a multi-stage Dockerfile that reduces image size by at least 50% compared to a single-stage build.

items: Create a multi-stage Dockerfile
Compare image sizes before and after
Add a .dockerignore file

quiz.question: What is a multi-stage build?
options: Using multiple FROM statements to create smaller final images
quiz.explanation: Multi-stage builds use multiple FROM statements, copying only needed artifacts from build stages to the final image.

quiz.question: What is a distroless image?
options: An image with no base layer
An image with only the runtime and app, no shell or package manager
quiz.explanation: Distroless images contain only your application and its runtime dependencies — no shell, package manager, or other tools.

quiz.question: How do you copy artifacts from a build stage?
quiz.explanation: The COPY --from=<stage_name> instruction copies files from a named build stage.

quiz.question: What is the optimal Dockerfile instruction order?
quiz.explanation: Putting least-frequently-changing instructions first maximizes layer cache hits.

quiz.question: What does a .dockerignore file do?
options: Excludes files and directories from the build context
quiz.explanation: .dockerignore specifies files/directories to exclude from the build context, reducing build time and image size.

quiz.question: Why use 'COPY package*.json ./' before 'COPY . .'?
options: To cache the npm install layer separately from source code changes
quiz.explanation: Copying package.json first and running npm install before copying source code means dependency layers are cached unless package.json changes.

quiz.question: What is the 'scratch' base image?
options: A completely empty image — the smallest possible base
quiz.explanation: scratch is Docker's empty base image — it contains absolutely nothing. Used for statically-compiled binaries.

quiz.question: How does Alpine Linux reduce image size?
options: It uses musl libc and busybox instead of glibc and coreutils
quiz.explanation: Alpine uses musl libc and busybox, which are much smaller than glibc and standard GNU coreutils.

quiz.question: What is BuildKit's --mount=type=cache?
options: A persistent cache mount shared between builds
quiz.explanation: --mount=type=cache creates a persistent cache that persists across builds, useful for package manager caches.

quiz.question: What is the benefit of smaller Docker images?
options: They use less memory at runtime
Faster build, push, pull, and deploy; smaller attack surface
They are more secure by default
quiz.explanation: Smaller images are faster to build, push, pull, and deploy. They also have a smaller attack surface.

lessons.title: Capstone: Containerize a Full-Stack App
lessons.description: Put it all together: containerize a full-stack application with frontend, backend, and database using Docker Compose.

blocks.content: Capstone: Containerize a Full-Stack App
This capstone brings together everything you've learned about Docker: images, containers, networking, volumes, security, and Docker Compose.

items: Complete all Docker lessons 01-20 first.
Designing a multi-container architecture
Docker Compose for local development
Environment management (dev vs prod)
Health checks and restart policies
Use Docker Compose for multi-container apps
Health checks prevent routing to unhealthy containers
Restart policies ensure availability

blocks.code:
version: '3.8'
services:
  frontend:
    build: ./frontend
    ports: ["3000:3000"]
    depends_on:
      backend:
        condition: service_healthy
  backend:
    build: ./backend
    ports: ["8000:8000"]
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://user:pass@db:5432/app
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "curl", "-f", "http://localhost:8000/health"]
      interval: 30s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 3
  db:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    volumes:
      - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: user
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: pass
      POSTGRES_DB: app
volumes:
  pgdata:

quiz.question: What is Docker Compose used for?
quiz.explanation: Docker Compose is a tool for defining and running multi-container Docker applications using a YAML file.

quiz.question: What does 'depends_on' with 'condition: service_healthy' do?
options: Starts the dependency after the main service
Waits for the dependency to be healthy before starting
quiz.explanation: depends_on with service_healthy waits until the dependency's health check passes before starting the dependent service.

quiz.question: How do you persist database data in Docker Compose?
options: Store it in the container filesystem
quiz.explanation: Named volumes persist data across container restarts and removals.

quiz.question: What is a health check in Docker?
options: A command that checks if a container is healthy
quiz.explanation: A health check runs a command periodically to determine if the container is functioning properly.

quiz.question: What restart policy keeps a container always running?
quiz.explanation: restart: unless-stopped keeps the container running unless it was explicitly stopped.

quiz.question: How do you pass environment variables in docker-compose.yml?
quiz.explanation: The 'environment' key in docker-compose.yml sets environment variables for a service.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of the 'build' key in docker-compose.yml?
options: Builds the image from a Dockerfile
Downloads an image from Docker Hub
quiz.explanation: The 'build' key specifies a directory containing a Dockerfile to build the image from.

quiz.question: How do you run Docker Compose in detached mode?
quiz.explanation: The -d flag runs containers in detached (background) mode.

quiz.question: What does 'docker-compose down' do?
options: Stops and removes containers, networks, and volumes (unless specified)
quiz.explanation: docker-compose down stops and removes containers, networks, and default networks. Use -v to also remove volumes.

quiz.question: How do you scale a service in Docker Compose?
quiz.explanation: The --scale flag scales a service to the specified number of replicas.
